analysis.one_liner: Requires police agencies to report detailed data on every use of deadly force, with funding penalties for refusing.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in the House Judiciary Committee and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the Justice Department to set rules forcing federal, state, and local police agencies to report detailed information every time an officer uses deadly force — who was killed, their race, gender, and age, what happened, and the agency's explanation. The data would be published publicly, with names kept private. States or cities that refused to comply would lose 10% of their federal Byrne police grant money. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The public would gain a complete, government-verified national record of police deadly force — currently the federal government's counts are known to be incomplete — letting communities, journalists, and researchers see patterns by race, age, and circumstance. Families of people killed by police would have their cases counted in official statistics. Who pays: police agencies bear the cost of collecting and submitting detailed reports on every incident, and governments that refuse would lose 10% of their Byrne grant funds.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require the Attorney General to issue rules requiring all law enforcement agencies to report detailed information on every use of deadly force, including the race, gender, age, and perceived religion of the person killed, the circumstances, and the agency's explanation [S2, S3].

The Bureau of Justice Statistics would have to publish the data and make it available to the public, so journalists, researchers, and communities could see patterns without relying on unofficial tallies [S3].
States or local governments that fail to substantially comply would lose 10% of their Byrne Justice Assistance Grant funds the following year, giving the mandate teeth [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Police agencies and the state/local governments that fund them, through new reporting obligations and possible 10% Byrne grant cuts for noncompliance.
analysis.who_pays_short: Police agencies and governments that refuse

drawbacks.text: The bill requires federal, state, and local agencies to collect detailed data on every deadly-force incident, which means administrative work and reporting burdens for thousands of police departments, and it withholds 10% of Byrne grant funds from governments that fail to comply [S2, S3].

The bill withholds officer and victim names from public release and exempts the data from Freedom of Information Act requests, so journalists and researchers could not use the dataset to identify individuals involved in specific shootings [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a national, standardized record of every police killing, published with privacy protections — comes at a modest cost: paperwork for police agencies and a 10% funding reduction for governments that refuse to report. Those are reasonable prices for the only reliable way to measure how often police use deadly force and against whom. The bill died without a hearing, so the public continues to rely on incomplete official counts and unofficial trackers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and its Crime Subcommittee on the day it was introduced, and no hearing or vote ever happened before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 3, 2019 and referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee and its Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security [S1, S5].
The action history shows no further activity after the referrals — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 with the bill still stuck in committee [S5].
It attracted 54 cosponsors, all Democrats, but never advanced [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies are better off: they were never required to report deadly-force data, and no agency faces the 10% Byrne grant penalty. The public lost a national record of police killings.

for.name: Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 3, 2019 and championed the deadly-force data reporting requirement [S1, S3].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chairman Jerrold Nadler (D-NY) and committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the two-year Congress, leaving it to die in committee [S5].

against.name: Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on introduction day and took no recorded action on the bill [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 54 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican supported the bill; with Democrats holding the House majority, the decisive barrier was that the committee never moved it, not a floor vote [S4, S5].

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (federal, state, and local)
industries.note: The bill imposes a new reporting duty on every police agency, backed by a 10% cut to Byrne grant funds for noncompliance, but it does not restrict how officers use force [S2, S3].

industries.industry: State and local governments receiving Byrne Justice Assistance Grants
industries.note: Governments that fail to report would lose 10% of these Justice Department grant funds the following year [S2].
